subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science - Biology Bioenergetics Reading
subtitle: Reading passages for photosynthesis, respiration, practical work and data interpretation.
description: A reading pack for KS3 biology bioenergetics. Passages focus on core explanations, practical methods, data interpretation and common misconceptions from the source study pack.

data.sourcePassage: Photosynthesis is the process used by plants and algae to make glucose. It happens mainly in leaves, inside cell structures called chloroplasts. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, a green pigment that absorbs light energy. The reactants are carbon dioxide and water. Carbon dioxide enters the leaf through stomata, while water is brought from the roots through veins. The products are glucose and oxygen. Glucose is a sugar that stores chemical energy. Plants use it for respiration, storage as starch, making cellulose for cell walls, making proteins when mineral ions are available, and moving sugars to growing parts. Oxygen leaves the leaf through stomata. Photosynthesis matters because it provides food molecules for plants and algae, produces oxygen for many organisms, and starts most food chains.

questions.question: Name the two reactants in photosynthesis.
questions.modelAnswer: The reactants are carbon dioxide and water.

questions.question: Where does photosynthesis happen mainly in plants?
questions.modelAnswer: Photosynthesis happens mainly in leaves, inside chloroplasts.

questions.question: Explain why chlorophyll is important for photosynthesis.
questions.modelAnswer: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, which is needed to change carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

questions.question: Give two ways plants use glucose after it is made.
questions.modelAnswer: Plants use glucose in respiration and can store it as starch. They can also make cellulose, proteins or transport sugars to growing parts.

questions.question: Why do animals depend directly or indirectly on photosynthesis?
questions.modelAnswer: Animals depend on photosynthesis because plants and algae make glucose that becomes food in food chains, and photosynthesis produces oxygen used in aerobic respiration.

data.sourcePassage: A starch test can show whether a leaf has made starch after being in the light. Before the test, a plant is often destarched by keeping it in the dark for 24 to 48 hours. This makes the plant use up stored starch in respiration, so any starch found later is more likely to have been made during the investigation. A leaf is dipped in hot water to kill it and stop reactions. It is then placed in ethanol in a hot water bath. Ethanol removes chlorophyll, making the colour change easier to see, but it is flammable so it must not be heated directly over a flame. The leaf is rinsed in warm water, then iodine solution is added. Iodine stays brown-orange if starch is absent and turns blue-black if starch is present.

questions.question: What colour does iodine turn when starch is present?
questions.modelAnswer: Iodine turns blue-black when starch is present.

questions.question: Why is a plant destarched before a starch test?
options: To use up old stored starch
To make the leaf absorb oxygen
To increase the number of stomata
questions.modelAnswer: Destarching uses up old stored starch before the investigation.

questions.question: Explain why ethanol is used in the starch test.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethanol removes chlorophyll from the leaf so the iodine colour change is easier to see.

questions.question: Why must ethanol be heated in a hot water bath rather than directly over a flame?
questions.modelAnswer: Ethanol is flammable, so direct heating with a flame would be unsafe.

questions.question: How could a variegated leaf provide evidence that chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis?
questions.modelAnswer: The green areas contain chlorophyll and can turn blue-black with iodine after light, showing starch was made. White areas have little or no chlorophyll and stay brown-orange, showing starch was not made there.

data.sourcePassage: A common KS3 photosynthesis investigation uses pondweed to estimate the rate of photosynthesis. The pondweed is placed in water with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, which provides carbon dioxide. A lamp is placed at a measured distance from the pondweed. After the pondweed has adjusted, oxygen bubbles are counted for a fixed time. The lamp can then be moved to different distances, such as 50 cm, 40 cm, 30 cm, 20 cm and 10 cm. In one set of results, the rate was 5 bubbles per minute at 50 cm, 8 at 40 cm, 12 at 30 cm, 11 at 20 cm and 22 at 10 cm. The general pattern is that the closer lamp gives a higher rate, but the 20 cm result is an anomaly because it is lower than the 30 cm result. Bubble counting is only an estimate because bubbles can vary in size.

questions.question: What substance is added to provide carbon dioxide in the pondweed investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: Sodium hydrogencarbonate solution is added to provide carbon dioxide.

questions.question: What was the dependent variable in the pondweed investigation?
options: The rate of oxygen bubbles per minute
questions.modelAnswer: The dependent variable was the rate of oxygen bubbles per minute.

questions.question: Describe the overall pattern in the pondweed data using numbers.
questions.modelAnswer: As the lamp moved closer, the rate generally increased, from 5 bubbles per minute at 50 cm to 22 bubbles per minute at 10 cm.

questions.question: Which result was the anomaly?
questions.modelAnswer: The 20 cm result was the anomaly because it was 11 bubbles per minute, lower than 12 bubbles per minute at 30 cm.

questions.question: Suggest two improvements to make the pondweed results more reliable or accurate.
questions.modelAnswer: Repeat each distance and calculate a mean to improve reliability. Use a gas syringe to measure oxygen volume more accurately, and control temperature because the lamp can heat the water.

data.sourcePassage: Respiration is a chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose. It is not the same as breathing. Breathing is ventilation: moving air into and out of the lungs. During exercise, muscle cells need more energy, so respiration increases. The body responds by increasing breathing rate, breathing depth and heart rate. This helps supply more oxygen and glucose to muscle cells and remove extra carbon dioxide. In a step-up investigation, pulse rate increased immediately after exercise and then decreased during recovery. Student B, for example, rose from 80 beats per minute at rest to 148 immediately after exercise, then fell to 88 after three minutes. If exercise is very intense, oxygen supply may not meet demand, so muscle cells can respire anaerobically. This produces lactic acid and releases less energy than aerobic respiration.

questions.question: What is respiration?
questions.modelAnswer: Respiration is a chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose.

questions.question: Which statement best describes breathing?
options: Moving air into and out of the lungs
Releasing energy from glucose in cells
Making glucose from carbon dioxide and water
questions.modelAnswer: Breathing is ventilation: moving air into and out of the lungs.

questions.question: Explain why heart rate increases during exercise.
questions.modelAnswer: Heart rate increases so blood can deliver oxygen and glucose to muscles more quickly and remove carbon dioxide from respiring cells.

questions.question: Use Student B's data to describe recovery after exercise.
questions.modelAnswer: Student B's pulse fell from 148 beats per minute immediately after exercise to 88 beats per minute after three minutes.

questions.question: Why can intense exercise lead to lactic acid build-up?
questions.modelAnswer: During intense exercise, oxygen supply may not meet demand, so some muscle cells respire anaerobically. This changes glucose into lactic acid and releases less energy.

data.sourcePassage: A limiting factor is a factor that stops a process from increasing because it is in shortest supply or unsuitable. For photosynthesis, the main limiting factors are light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. At low light intensity, increasing light usually increases the rate because more light energy is available for chlorophyll to absorb. At higher light intensity, the graph may level off. This plateau shows that another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, has become limiting. Temperature also affects fermentation in yeast because fermentation is controlled by enzymes. In one yeast investigation, carbon dioxide production rose from 4 cm3 at 10 degrees Celsius to 38 cm3 at 40 degrees Celsius, then dropped to 8 cm3 at 50 degrees Celsius. Low temperature slows enzyme reactions, while very high temperature can stop enzymes working properly.

questions.question: Name the three main limiting factors for photosynthesis.
questions.modelAnswer: The main limiting factors are light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature.

questions.question: What does a plateau on a photosynthesis rate graph usually show?
questions.modelAnswer: A plateau shows that another factor has become limiting.

questions.question: Use the yeast data to describe the pattern from 10 degrees Celsius to 40 degrees Celsius.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide production increased from 4 cm3 at 10 degrees Celsius to 38 cm3 at 40 degrees Celsius.

questions.question: Explain why carbon dioxide production fell at 50 degrees Celsius.
questions.modelAnswer: At very high temperatures, enzymes in yeast may stop working properly, so fermentation decreases and less carbon dioxide is produced.

questions.question: Why might adding carbon dioxide to a greenhouse not help much if light intensity is very low?
questions.modelAnswer: If light intensity is very low, light is the limiting factor. Adding carbon dioxide will not greatly increase photosynthesis until enough light energy is available.
